newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: U.S. to "engage" with S. Asia in new Clinton term.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to "engage" with S. Asia in new Clinton term.

text.p: The United States plans to focus renewed attention on South Asia in President Bill Clinton's second term, a U.S. official said on Wednesday.

"In the second Clinton administration we certainly expect that there will be further engagement with the South Asia region," Assistant Secretary of State for South Asian Affairs Robin Raphel told a news conference in Islamabad.

"We've been saying for the last some years that South Asia is definitely a region of growing importance to the United States, to the West in general and also to Asia, in economic terms, security terms and so on," she said.
"The Clinton administration...wishes to engage in particular with India and Pakistan, but also with other countries in the region on a range of issues, commercial and otherwise."
Raphel was speaking during a two-day visit to Pakistan before attending a meeting in Dhaka of U.S. ambassadors in South Asia. Her tour will also take her to India and Sri Lanka.

She said she had had good talks with President Farooq Leghari, chief of army staff General Jehangir Karamat, Foreign Minister Sahibzada Yaqoob Khan, finance and economic affairs adviser Shahid Javed Burki and other Pakistani officials.
Raphel said the discussions had covered a range of bilateral issues and Afghanistan, but gave no details.
She said nuclear non-proliferation was a regular item on Washington's regional agenda.
"We would like to see both Pakistan and India sign the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, sign the Non-Proliferation Treaty, and generally accede to international treaties on these matters," she said.

India and Pakistan both deny possessing nuclear weapons, but U.S. officials believe they could assemble them quickly. India exploded a nuclear device in 1974, but has not carried out a nuclear test since then. Pakistan has carried out no tests.
"Both countries have exercised restraint in these issues, by not testing for example," Raphel said. "So the glass is not totally empty, but there is a way to go in that dialogue."
She voiced hope that both governments would be helpful in forthcoming talks on an agreement to ban fissile materials.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since their independence from Britain in 1947, two of them over Kashmir.

Raphel reiterated the U.S. position on the Kashmir issue, saying Washington regarded the Himalayan region as disputed territory and was ready to assist India and Pakistan in finding a negotiated solution, but only if asked to do so.
"India and Pakistan need to negotiate a resolution, but they do need to take into account the wishes of the Kashmiri people in doing so," she said.

Relations between India and Pakistan have worsened since the 1990 outbreak of a Moslem separatist revolt in the two-thirds of Kashmir controlled by New Delhi. Pakistan denies Indian charges that it gives the Kashmiri guerrillas guns, money and training.
